# No Vestige of a Beginning

Pick up any stone — the beach one you pocketed and never returned, the gray lump on the windowsill that gets lifted every time the sill gets dusted. Notice its temperature first: cool in the shade, holding the afternoon in the sun. Then its weight, the way it sits in your palm with total indifference. Nothing you do will register in its biography. Your birthday, your worst day, the whole loud century — none of it will appear in the record this object keeps.

The indifference is an illusion of scale. The stone is not motionless; it is merely slower than you. Speed the film up and the picture changes: mountains ripple like kelp in a current, coastlines breathe in and out, whole ranges rise, shrug, and dissolve into rivers that carry them to the sea the way sugar goes into coffee. At high speed, geology is weather. A rock is not a thing but an event — a wave so slow that we stand on it and call it land.

Human eyes evolved for foxes and falling fruit, for things that move at the speed of consequences. Anything slower than a season slid beneath our perception and stayed there for most of our history. We are, in this one respect, nearsighted animals. It took us an embarrassingly long time to work out how long "a long time" is, and the discovery was made the way discoveries usually are: by someone who noticed something out of place and refused to look away.

On a June day in 1788, three men rowed along the Berwickshire coast of Scotland to look at a cliff. James Hutton was a farmer with a compulsion about rocks; John Playfair, a mathematician, had come along to see; James Hall, a wealthy friend, would later spend years in a furnace-lit laboratory proving Hutton right. They landed beneath a promontory called Siccar Point and climbed to the cliff's edge, and there they found two architectures stacked in a single rock face. Below lay beds of gray sandstone standing on end, tipped vertical, folded like a squeezed accordion. Above them, resting on their severed edges, lay red sandstone beds lying almost flat — serene, as if nothing had ever happened.

Something had happened. The vertical layers had once been mud on a quiet seabed. Compressed, buried, then caught in the collision of continents, they had been folded and hoisted into mountains — the Caledonian range, which in its day stood as tall as the Himalayas do now. And then the rain began. Time enough passed for an entire mountain range to be eaten down to its roots. The roots sank; the sea returned; new sand drifted over the stumps and hardened into the red rock on top. Then the whole parcel — roots and fill together — was tilted gently and lifted above the waves, and the sea is gnawing at it again, one winter at a time.

Playfair, who wrote the account we have, admitted that his mind "seemed to grow giddy by looking so far back into the abyss of time." He and his companions became aware, he said, of how much farther reason may go than imagination can venture to follow. That sentence is the birth certificate of deep time. The reasoning could carry Hutton to conclusions his own senses could not follow. It is one thing to say "millions of years." It is another to stand inside the proof, with the North Sea wind coming off the water, and feel the floor of human intuition give way.

Here is the strangest part. Between the vertical strata and the horizontal ones lies a gap of roughly sixty million years — and no rock records it. There is nothing there but the surface the mountain range once was: hills worn flat, drowned, and buried, like a sentence erased from a page with the indentation still legible. Hutton was reading an absence. Siccar Point is a library in which the most important chapter survives only as the burn mark where it used to be.

Hutton drew the obvious, scandalous conclusion. If ordinary processes — rain, frost, sediment, uplift — could erase a mountain range and file the evidence in plain sight, then the Earth must be immensely older than any human chronology, and there was no telling how much older, because nowhere in the rocks could he find "a vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end." No first page. No last. The Earth was not a stage set built recently for the benefit of the people standing on it. It was a machine with no dashboard and no odometer, running on slow.

The Grand Canyon teaches the same lesson at operatic scale. In its deepest gorge, flat-lying sandstone laid down about 525 million years ago rests directly on black crystalline rock almost 1.7 billion years old. Geologists call the contact the Great Unconformity, and it erases more than a billion years — a missing chapter longer than everything that survives. The rock record is mostly record of what is gone. Time writes in a library that periodically burns.

But *how* old? The nineteenth century's best physics said: not very. Lord Kelvin calculated how long a molten sphere the size of the Earth would take to cool to its present temperature and got a few tens of millions of years. Geologists ground their teeth and made do. Darwin, who needed eons for natural selection to sculpt an eye, complained in his letters and quietly arranged his theory around the shortage. Kelvin was a genius, and he was wrong, and the reason he was wrong is the best part: he did not know the planet had a furnace in every grain. Rocks are faintly radioactive. The Earth runs warm on the decay of uranium and thorium and potassium — heat Kelvin could not have budgeted for, generated by the very element that would shortly hand us a clock.

In 1904 a young Ernest Rutherford rose to lecture on the age of the Earth and spotted Kelvin in the audience, elderly and dozing. Rutherford later confessed that he panicked. But he remembered that Kelvin had left himself a window: the Earth could be older only if some new source of heat existed. Rutherford invoked the window aloud; Kelvin, the story goes, opened one eye; the lecture survived. The new source of heat was real, and it came with a bonus. Radioactivity did not merely warm the planet. It ticked.

The clock works like this. Uranium decays to lead at a fixed rate — half gone every 4.5 billion years, whether anyone is watching or not. Find a mineral that sealed itself shut at birth, count the daughter lead against the parent uranium, and you know how long the seal has held. The best of all such minerals is zircon: a tiny, hardy crystal whose lattice admits uranium but refuses lead, so that any lead found inside a zircon is lead the uranium has confessed to making. Zircon is nearly indestructible. Grind its parent rock to mud, melt its mountain, drown it in a sea of sand, and the crystal rides through all of it, holding its date.

In the Jack Hills of Western Australia, zircons have been found that crystallized about 4.4 billion years ago. No *rock* on Earth is older than roughly 4.03 billion; the planet's original crust has been recycled beyond recovery. These crystals are older than every rock that survives — orphans who outlived every parent, washed into younger sediments over and over as the continents chewed themselves up. And their chemistry holds a surprise: the oxygen locked inside them is the oxygen of a world touched by liquid water. The Hadean, the hell of the early Earth, apparently cooled into oceans astonishingly fast. Some of the oldest sentences in the planetary record are about water.

- Siccar Point, Berwickshire coast, Scotland.
- June 1788: Hutton, John Playfair (mathematician), and James Hall sailed along the coast; landed at Siccar Point.
- Unconformity: vertical Silurian greywackes (~460–430 Ma) overlain by sub-horizontal Devonian Old Red Sandstone (~370–350 Ma). Gap ~60–100 million years. The vertical strata were once the roots of the Caledonian mountain range (formed when Baltica/Laurentia/Avalonia collided—similar scale to the Himalayas).
- Playfair's line: "the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far back into the abyss of time." (From Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory of the Earth, 1802.)
- Hutton's closing line in the 1788 paper: "we find no vestige of a beginning,—no prospect of an end."
- Hutton's uniformitarianism; later Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830–33); "the present is the key to the past."
- Kelvin's objection: physics said Earth too young (cooling calculations, ~20–100 Myr); resolved by radioactivity—both as heat source and as clock.
- Ernest Rutherford, 1904ish, dating with radioactivity; Bertram Boltwood first uranium-lead dates (~1907); Arthur Holmes developed geologic timescale.
- Oldest rocks: Acasta Gneiss (~4.03 Ga), Nuvvuagittuq belt disputed (~4.28 Ga). Oldest minerals: Jack Hills zircons, Western Australia, up to ~4.4 Ga (Wilde et al. 2001).
- Zircon: ZrSiO4; incorporates uranium, rejects lead at formation—so lead present is radiogenic; uranium-238 half-life ~4.47 billion years; a self-contained clock.
- Oxygen isotope ratios in Jack Hills zircons (Mojzsis, Harrison) suggest interaction with liquid water → cool early Earth, oceans within a few hundred Myr of formation.
- Earth age ~4.54 Ga (Claire Patterson 1956, meteorites, Canyon Diablo).
- Moon-forming impact ~4.5 Ga; Hadean eon; Late Heavy Bombardment debated.
- Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi (1883): Earth's history as Eiffel Tower; human history as "a film of skin" of paint on the tower's pinnacle—"so shallow that a fly could walk over it." Approximately: "The face of the tower... and the observer... the procession of geological ages... and the paint on the top." Let me recall the actual quote: "If the Eiffel tower were now representing the world's age, the skin of paint on the pinnacle, at which a person would slide up with a little difficulty, would represent man's share of the age; and anybody would perceive that the skin was what the tower was built for. I reckon they would, I dunno." Yes, close to that—the famous last bit "and anybody would perceive that that skin was what the tower was built for. I reckon they would, I dunno." I can quote the gist carefully.
- Holocene: began ~11,700 years ago; interglacial of the Quaternary ice age; glacial cycles ~100 kyr (Milankovitch: eccentricity ~100k/400k, obliquity ~41k, precession ~23k/19k—conveniently roughly matching glacial rhythm).
- Last Glacial Maximum ~26.5–19 kya; sea level ~120 m lower; land bridges: Beringia, Doggerland (North Sea), Sunda shelf.
- Agriculture ~12–10 kya (Levant, then China, Mesoamerica, Andes, New Guinea); writing ~5.2 kya (cuneiform ~3200 BCE, also Egyptian); Great Pyramid ~4.5 kya. All human cities within the Holocene.
- Anthropocene: term by Paul Crutzen (~2000, popularized; Eugene Stoermer earlier coined it). Great Acceleration post-1950. Stratigraphic markers: radionuclides (plutonium-239/240) global spike from bomb tests (~1952 onward, peak 1960s), plastics, aluminum, fly ash, concrete, nitrogen from Haber-Bosch, chicken bones (broiler chicken—almost all chicken bones on Earth now from post-1940s breed; "Gallus gallus domesticus" techno-fossil; Carys Bennett paper on broiler chicken as marker), plastic "plastiglomerates" (Patricia Corcoran).
- Anthropogenic mass exceeding biomass: Elhacham et al., Nature 2020—anthropogenic mass ~1.1 teratonne; exceeds all living biomass (~1.1 Tt dry?)—actually the study said 2020 the anthropogenic mass (1.2 Tt) surpassed overall living biomass on Earth (~1.1 Tt). I can phrase it carefully: "human-made mass—concrete, brick, asphalt—recently surpassed all the living biomass on Earth."
